name: Spanish Grammar Drill
credits: Hand-curated to complement the vocab path. Pedagogically sequenced from concrete (present indicative) to abstract (subjunctive). Verb patterns checked against RAE conjugation tables; common-error notes drawn from published L2-Spanish error corpora.

units.title: Present tense — regular -ar verbs
units.goal: Conjugate any regular -ar verb in the present indicative.
units.explanation: Spanish regular -ar verbs follow a single pattern. Drop the -ar from the infinitive and add the personal ending. This pattern covers roughly half of all Spanish verbs.
common_errors: Forgetting the accent on the vosotros form (-áis, not -ais)
Adding a subject pronoun when none is needed — 'Hablo español' is complete; 'yo' is for emphasis
Using English-style auxiliary 'do/does' — 'Do you work?' is just '¿Trabajas?', not '¿Tú haces trabajar?'

units.title: Present tense — regular -er and -ir verbs
units.goal: Conjugate any regular -er or -ir verb in the present indicative.
units.explanation: Regular -er and -ir verbs share endings in four of six persons. They only differ in the nosotros and vosotros forms: -emos/-éis for -er, -imos/-ís for -ir. Once you learn one pattern, the other is a small mutation.

examples.target: Yo como pan todos los días.

examples.en: We live in a small house.

examples.target: Mis hijos escriben cartas a la abuela.
examples.en: My children write letters to grandma.

common_errors: Using -ar endings on -er/-ir verbs ('yo como', not 'yo coma')
Mixing nosotros forms — 'comemos' (we eat) vs 'vivimos' (we live); never 'comimos' for present
Dropping the accent on -éis / -ís for vosotros

units.title: Ser vs Estar — choosing the right 'to be'
units.goal: Pick ser or estar correctly in the most common contexts.
units.explanation: Spanish splits English 'to be' into two verbs. Ser describes identity, origin, defining traits and time. Estar describes location, mood, ongoing condition, and the result of a change. The mnemonic DOCTOR (Description, Occupation, Characteristic, Time, Origin, Relationship) covers ser; PLACE (Position, Location, Action in progress, Condition, Emotion) covers estar.

examples.target: El libro es interesante. (defining trait → ser)
Madrid está en España, pero es la capital. (location → estar; identity → ser)
examples.en: Madrid is in Spain, but it's the capital.

common_errors: Using ser for location of objects/people — 'El libro está en la mesa', never 'es en la mesa'
Using estar for nationality or profession — 'Soy mexicano' (ser), not 'Estoy mexicano'
Same adjective changes meaning: 'Es aburrido' (he is boring) vs 'Está aburrido' (he is bored). Bueno, malo, listo, rico all behave this way.

units.title: Gender of nouns & adjective agreement
units.goal: Predict noun gender, choose the matching article, and agree adjectives in gender.
units.explanation: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, even inanimate ones. Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine; -a, -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad are usually feminine. Articles and adjectives must match the noun's gender. Common exceptions: el día, el mapa, el problema (masculine despite -a); la mano, la foto, la radio (feminine despite -o).

pattern.infinitive: el libro rojo / la casa roja

endings.invariant (ends in -e/-consonant): no change for gender, +s/+es for plural

examples.target: El problema es difícil. (problema is masculine!)
Mi madre es alta y rubia.
examples.en: My mother is tall and blonde.

common_errors: Assuming -a always means feminine — 'el día', 'el mapa', 'el problema', 'el tema' break the rule
Forgetting to agree adjectives — 'la casa blanco' is wrong; must be 'la casa blanca'
Adjectives ending in -e (grande, inteligente, verde) don't change for gender, but do add -s for plural

units.title: Plural nouns & adjectives
units.goal: Form the plural of any noun and matching adjective.
units.explanation: Add -s to nouns ending in a vowel: libro → libros. Add -es to nouns ending in a consonant: ciudad → ciudades. Words ending in -z change to -ces: luz → luces. Words ending in stressed vowels often add -es: rubí → rubíes. Adjectives follow the same rules and must match the noun's number.

examples.target: Los lunes son difíciles. (lunes stays lunes)

common_errors: Adding -s to consonant-ending nouns — 'ciudads' is wrong; correct is 'ciudades'
Forgetting the z→c shift — 'luzs' is wrong, 'luces' is correct
Not agreeing adjectives in number — 'los libros nuevo' should be 'los libros nuevos'
Pluralizing days ending in -s unnecessarily ('los lunes', not 'los luneses')

units.title: Possessives — short & long forms
units.goal: Use the short (mi, tu, su) and long (mío, tuyo, suyo) possessive forms correctly.
units.explanation: Short possessives go BEFORE the noun and agree only in number (and gender for nuestro/vuestro). Long possessives go AFTER the noun or stand alone, and agree in both gender and number. 'Su' is ambiguous (his/her/your-formal/their); add 'de él/ella/usted/ellos' to disambiguate.

endings.long forms: mío, tuyo, suyo, nuestro, vuestro, suyo (with -a/-os/-as agreement)

examples.en: A friend of mine arrived yesterday.

examples.target: Su coche es de ella. (clarifying su)
examples.en: Her car (literally: her car is hers).

common_errors: Using long form in pre-noun position — 'mío libro' is wrong; should be 'mi libro' or 'el libro mío'
Forgetting that 'mi' has no gender — 'mi' before any noun, but 'nuestro' agrees in gender
Assuming 'su' means only 'his' — it can mean his/her/your-formal/their; context or 'de + pronoun' disambiguates

units.title: Direct & indirect object pronouns
units.goal: Replace direct and indirect objects with pronouns, in the correct order and position.
units.explanation: Direct object pronouns (me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las) replace 'whom/what' the verb acts on. Indirect objects (me, te, le, nos, os, les) replace 'to whom / for whom'. Both go BEFORE a conjugated verb but can attach to an infinitive or gerund. When both appear together, indirect comes first, and 'le/les + lo/la/los/las' becomes 'se + lo/la/los/las'.

endings.direct (me/you/him-it/her-it/us/you-pl/t: me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las
endings.indirect (to me/you/him-her-you/us/you-p: me, te, le, nos, os, les
endings.order with conjugated verb: indirect before direct, both before verb
endings.le + lo/la → se + lo/la: Le doy el libro → Se lo doy

examples.en: I see María. → I see her.
I buy the book. → I buy it.

examples.target: Le doy el libro a Juan. → Se lo doy.
examples.en: I give the book to Juan. → I give it to him.

common_errors: Using 'lo' for a feminine direct object — 'la veo' for 'I see her', not 'lo veo'
Forgetting le→se before lo/la — 'le lo doy' is ungrammatical; must be 'se lo doy'
Wrong order — 'lo me das' is wrong; should be 'me lo das' (indirect always first)
Le/lo confusion (leísmo): 'Lo veo' for masculine person is standard; 'Le veo' is dialectal Spain Spanish only

units.title: Reflexive verbs — me, te, se
units.goal: Recognise and conjugate reflexive verbs for daily routine and changes of state.
units.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe actions done to oneself. The infinitive ends in -se: levantarse (to get oneself up), llamarse (to call oneself). Conjugate the verb normally, but place the matching reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) before the conjugated form. Many become reflexive only to mean a change of state: dormir (to sleep) vs dormirse (to fall asleep).

examples.en: What's your name? — My name is Ana.

examples.target: Voy a ducharme. / Me voy a duchar.

common_errors: Forgetting the reflexive pronoun — 'levanto a las siete' is wrong; must be 'me levanto'
Wrong pronoun for the subject — 'me llamas' (you call me) vs 'te llamas' (your name is)
Mixing reflexive and non-reflexive meaning — 'duermo' (I sleep) vs 'me duermo' (I fall asleep)
Forgetting that body parts use the definite article, not a possessive: 'me lavo las manos' (I wash my hands), not 'lavo mis manos'

units.title: Preterite tense — completed past actions
units.goal: Conjugate regular verbs and the most common irregulars in the preterite.
units.explanation: The preterite reports a completed action with a defined endpoint: 'I ate', 'we went', 'they finished'. Regular endings: -ar verbs take -é/-aste/-ó/-amos/-asteis/-aron; -er and -ir share -í/-iste/-ió/-imos/-isteis/-ieron. Ser and ir share the same preterite (fui, fuiste, fue…). Hacer is hice, hiciste, hizo (note the z) — the 'tener-style' irregular group (tener→tuve, estar→estuve, poner→puse, poder→pude, saber→supe) all share the same unstressed endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron.

endings.ser/ir (same forms): fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron
endings.hacer: hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron

examples.en: Yesterday I spoke with my mother.

examples.target: Comimos en un restaurante muy bueno.
examples.en: We ate at a very good restaurant.
I went to the cinema on Saturday.
What did you do last night?

common_errors: Forgetting the accent on -é and -ó — 'hable' (subjunctive) vs 'hablé' (preterite I)
Same nosotros form for present and preterite in -ar/-ir verbs: 'hablamos' is both 'we speak' and 'we spoke' — context disambiguates
Confusing fui (ser/ir) and fue (he was / he went) — same form, no way to tell apart without context
Saying 'hizo' as 'hico' — the c→z spelling change keeps the soft sound before o

units.title: Imperfect tense — past habits & descriptions
units.goal: Conjugate regular and the three irregular imperfect verbs (ser, ir, ver).
units.explanation: The imperfect describes past habits, repeated actions, ongoing background, and 'used to / was -ing' meaning. It has only three irregular verbs (ser, ir, ver); everything else is fully predictable. -ar verbs: -aba/-abas/-aba/-ábamos/-abais/-aban. -er and -ir share -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-íais/-ían.

pattern.infinitive: hablar / comer / vivir / ser / ir / ver
pattern.stem: habl- / com- / viv- / er- / ib- / ve-

endings.ser: era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran
endings.ir: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban
endings.ver: veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían

examples.target: De niño vivía en el campo.
examples.en: As a child I lived in the countryside.

examples.target: Mi abuela cocinaba todos los domingos.
examples.en: My grandmother used to cook every Sunday.

examples.target: Cuando era joven, iba a la playa.
examples.en: When I was young, I would go to the beach.
While I was studying, I would listen to music.
I would watch TV every night.

common_errors: Confusing yo and él forms — they're identical (hablaba, comía); subject pronouns or context disambiguate
Forgetting the accent on -íamos / -íais — 'comiamos' is wrong; correct is 'comíamos'
Treating ver as fully irregular — only the stem keeps the e (veía, veías) but endings are regular -er/-ir
Using imperfect for a single completed event — 'I ate at 8' is 'comí a las 8' (preterite), not 'comía a las 8'

units.title: Preterite vs Imperfect — when to use each
units.goal: Decide between preterite and imperfect when narrating in the past.
units.explanation: Preterite reports what HAPPENED: completed, bounded, single events (or repeated a stated number of times). Imperfect describes what WAS happening or USED to happen: background, habits, descriptions, age, weather, time, and ongoing emotional/physical states. A narrative usually combines them: imperfect sets the scene, preterite advances the plot. Time markers help: ayer/anoche/de repente/dos veces → preterite; siempre/cada día/mientras/cuando era → imperfect.

endings.preterite (what happened): completed action, defined endpoint, sequence of events
endings.imperfect (what was happening): habit, description, ongoing state, scene-setting, age/time/weather in the past

examples.target: Cuando era niño, vivía en México. (description, habit → imperfect)
examples.en: When I was a child, I lived in Mexico.

examples.target: Ayer fui al cine y vi una película. (completed events → preterite)
examples.en: Yesterday I went to the cinema and watched a film.

examples.target: Llovía cuando salí de casa. (background + event → imperfect + preterite)
examples.en: It was raining when I left the house.

examples.target: Tenía diez años cuando me mudé. (age + event → imperfect + preterite)
examples.en: I was ten when I moved.

examples.target: Mi madre cocinaba mientras yo estudiaba. (parallel ongoing → both imperfect)
examples.en: My mother was cooking while I was studying.

common_errors: Using preterite for description/scene — 'It was sunny' is 'hacía sol', not 'hizo sol' (unless reporting a brief change)
Using imperfect for a single completed action — 'I ate breakfast at 8' is 'desayuné', not 'desayunaba'

Some verbs shift meaning: conocer-preterite = met for first time, conocer-imperfect = used to know; saber-preterite = found out, saber-imperfect = knew; poder-preterite = managed to, poder-imperfect = was able to
Forgetting that 'cuando + imperfect' usually pairs with preterite for the interrupting event

units.title: Subjunctive intro — querer que, esperar que (B1 bridge)
units.goal: Recognise the present subjunctive and use it after triggers of desire and emotion.
units.explanation: The subjunctive expresses subjectivity: wishes, doubt, emotion, judgments about a second subject. The most reliable A2-to-B1 trigger pattern is 'verb of wish/emotion + que + different subject + subjunctive'. To form regular present subjunctive: take the yo form of the present indicative, drop the -o, and add the 'opposite-vowel' endings (-ar verbs take -e endings; -er/-ir verbs take -a endings). Irregulars: ser → sea, ir → vaya, haber → haya, saber → sepa, dar → dé, estar → esté.

endings.triggers: querer que, esperar que, desear que, ojalá, es importante que, me alegra que

examples.en: I want you to speak more slowly.

examples.target: Es importante que estudies todos los días.
examples.en: It's important that you study every day.

common_errors: Using subjunctive when the subject doesn't change — 'Quiero hablar español' (same subject → infinitive), not 'Quiero que hable español'
Using indicative after 'que' with a wish — 'Quiero que hablas' is wrong; must be 'Quiero que hables'
Forgetting that 'ojalá' always triggers subjunctive, never indicative
Treating 'creo que' as a subjunctive trigger — in affirmative it takes indicative ('Creo que es bueno'); only negated ('No creo que sea bueno') triggers subjunctive
